awd_titl_txt: POSE: Phase I: Creation of an Open Source Ecosystem to Repurpose DNA Sequencers as an Automation Platform
awd_abstract_narration:
As DNA sequencing technology rapidly evolves, once state-of-the-art equipment, originally priced in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, often becomes obsolete in less than a decade. Consequently, thousands of DNA sequencers are being decommissioned and, without a clear use, are either discarded or sold on secondary markets at a fraction of their original cost. Despite being outdated for sequencing, these instruments still contain highly valuable components including precision robotics, advanced optics, temperature control, and microfluidic systems. With the right software, engineering support, and experimental framework, these components could be repurposed into powerful platforms for automating a wide range of modern biological assays, thereby accelerating research and discovery. In particular, the emerging field of spatial omics offers transformative insights into important biological processes such as cancer, neurodegeneration, and immune response, but is currently hindered by its reliance on commercial automation platforms that remain prohibitively expensive to many laboratories. This project addresses this challenge by establishing an open-source ecosystem that unites researchers, engineers, and developers working towards the common goal of transforming decommissioned DNA sequencers into flexible automation platforms. This initiative will improve throughput, increase accessibility, reduce electronic waste, and promote greater standardization in biological research.

This project builds upon PySeq, an open-source toolkit developed to control individual components within DNA sequencers, enabling their use in spatial omics and other biomedical research applications. The primary goal is to unlock the full potential of decommissioned DNA sequencers by creating an open-source ecosystem centered around PySeq, transforming these powerful but unused instruments into flexible platforms for laboratory automation. The project is realized through three main aims: (i) Engage directly with current PySeq users to establish a core community of contributors focused on developing control tools, protocols, and documentation; (ii) Collaborate with users and developers to establish sustainable governance structures that support long-term community development and open-source philosophy; and (iii) Expand the user base by disseminating technological knowledge, procedures, best practices, and new perspectives to researchers utilizing laboratory automation. Through the exchange of protocols, hardware modifications, maintenance procedures, and software tools, the overarching goal is to build a self-sustained community that will launch PySeq OSE as a robust platform that transforms once-obsolete instruments into powerful, accessible tools for modern science.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
During the award period, the PySeq Open-Source Ecosystem was renamed the ReGenSeq Open-Source Ecosystem (RGS OSE) to better reflect its vision of repurposing next generation sequencing systems with cohesive control software, experimental protocols, custom flow cells, and image analysis pipelines. The Phase I project assessed the emerging ecosystem around repurposed sequencing instruments by mapping its participants, identifying barriers to adoption and contribution, and determining the resources, partnerships, and governance needed for sustainable growth. This work advances the broader goal of extending the useful life of sophisticated scientific equipment, preserving the value of prior investments, and making advanced research capabilities accessible to more laboratories.

INTELLECTUAL MERIT

1. Ecosystem Mapping and Community Insights: Through the NSF POSE I-Corps training, we conducted more than 150 interviews with researchers, core facility staff, instrument owners, software developers, manufacturers, and suppliers to map the RGS OSE community. The interviews converged on a central finding: retired instruments and interested users both exist in substantial numbers, but no channel connects them. Core facilities, institutions, and manufacturers are actively retiring sequencers and are willing to place them with new users, while laboratories that would put them to work have no reliable way to learn what is available or how to arrange a transfer. Documentation, maintenance of retired equipment, and pathways for contributing software and protocols emerged as secondary obstacles. This finding set our priorities: cataloguing instrument availability, direct engagement with core facilities and suppliers, and the governance and contribution infrastructure needed to support users once instruments are placed.

2. Establishing Community Resources: To anchor the ecosystem in a single public location, we built a central website that serves as its hub, listing routes to access starter kits, flow cells, decommissioned sequencers, software, protocols. Supporting it, a dedicated ReGenSeq GitHub organization now hosts three software repositories, including a shared core library and a template that lets community members add support for new instrument models, all released under the MIT license. We also established a protocols.io workspace for sharing and refining experimental methods  and a YouTube channel for instructional material on instrument operation, maintenance, and experimental workflows. 

3. Strengthening Collaborative Software Development: Assessment of governance practices across comparable open-source projects, together with the POSE governance training, indicated that at the ecosystem's present scale decision-making is best held by a single founding maintainer while contribution remains fully open. We developed a set of Community Guidelines and a code of conduct that define how users report issues, propose changes, and contribute code, with all proposals handled openly through public repositories. Every proposed contribution is now tested automatically across multiple configurations before it can be accepted, with results reported directly to the contributor. The control software is also automatically deployed to the Python Package Index and the installation process has been streamlined for new users and developers.

BROADER IMPACTS

1. Expanding Access to Research Infrastructure: We established and began operating a working pathway between institutions retiring sequencing instruments and laboratories able to put them to use. During the award year three instruments were transferred to new research groups, and we advised additional institutions on identifying and repurposing equipment available on their own campuses. Each placement adds an active participant to the ecosystem: recipient laboratories test and refine protocols, report issues, and extend the software to their own applications, so that the community's shared resources grow with every instrument returned to service.

2. Training and Educational Outreach: We established partnerships and developed plans for hands-on workshops covering instrument operation, maintenance, software use, and experimental implementation. We also began organizing a community user meeting for researchers, developers, core facility staff, and suppliers to exchange technical experience and establish shared practices. Online protocols and instructional materials further support users who cannot attend in-person training.

3. Knowledge Dissemination and Community Building: We presented the RGS OSE and research enabled by repurposed sequencers at the Advances in Genome Biology and Technology conference, the annual meeting of the American Society of Human Genetics, and the Biology of Genomes conference. These presentations connected the project with researchers, core facilities managing retired instruments, prospective users, and potential ecosystem partners.
